nameStory: The 'largeflower' part is straightforward - this bellwort has the biggest blooms of all our New England bellworts! The 'bellwort' name comes from those droopy, bell-shaped yellow flowers that hang like little church bells from the stems. Some folks also call it 'merrybells' because the cheerful yellow blooms seem to dance and jingle in the spring breeze.
description: Largeflower bellwort is a graceful woodland wildflower that stands about 1-2 feet tall in our New England forests. It has an elegant, arching growth habit with oval leaves that seem to wrap partway around the stem. The plant's crowning glory is its droopy, bright yellow bell-shaped flowers that hang beneath the leaves like little lanterns. This spring ephemeral blooms early in the season before the forest canopy fills in completely.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow, droopy bell-shaped flowers hang singly from branch tips, usually hidden beneath the leaves. The petals are long and twisted, and the flowers are noticeably larger than other bellworts - about 1-2 inches long. They feel papery and delicate to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, pointed leaves are arranged alternately and appear to wrap partway around the stem (though they don't go all the way around). The leaves feel soft and slightly fuzzy underneath, with prominent parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: The plant has an elegant, arching form with stems that fork and bend gracefully. Multiple stems often grow from the same root system, creating small colonies that seem to flow through the forest understory.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces a three-chambered capsule that splits open when ripe, revealing several seeds. The fruit is triangular in cross-section and develops where the flowers were, still hanging beneath the leaves.

habitat: Look for largeflower bellwort in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with deep, organic soil. It thrives in the dappled shade of maple, beech, and birch forests, often growing alongside trout lily, wild ginger, and other spring wildflowers. You'll typically find it on gentle slopes and in protected valleys rather than exposed ridges.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for largeflower bellwort! The bright yellow bell-shaped flowers bloom from April through May, hanging beneath the emerging leaves like little lanterns. The whole plant is most visible now before the forest canopy leafs out completely.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and the plant focuses on seed production. The three-chambered seed capsules develop and the leaves remain green and photosynthetically active in the forest understory.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow and die back, and seed capsules split open to release seeds. The plant becomes much less noticeable as it prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. The plant survives underground via its rhizome system, waiting for spring's return.

funFact: Despite being called 'merrybells,' these flowers don't actually make any sound - but early botanists were so charmed by how they seemed to dance and sway in the slightest breeze that they imagined they could hear them chiming like tiny fairy bells!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with its smaller cousins, perfoliate bellwort and sessile bellwort. Remember: largeflower has the biggest, showiest yellow flowers and leaves that only partially wrap around the stem. Perfoliate bellwort's leaves go completely around the stem like a collar, while sessile bellwort has leaves that don't wrap around at all - they just sit directly on the stem.
contextualKnowledge: All bellworts were once classified in the lily family, but botanists now place them in their own family (Colchicaceae) based on genetic studies. Despite the family shuffle, they're still closely related to lilies and share many similar characteristics like their parallel-veined leaves and six-petaled flowers.
compareHints: Largeflower bellwort lives up to its name with flowers that are noticeably larger and more showy than either perfoliate or sessile bellwort. While all three have yellow droopy flowers, largeflower bellwort's blooms are the brightest and most conspicuous. The leaf attachment is the key difference: largeflower's leaves partially clasp the stem, perfoliate's leaves completely surround it, and sessile's leaves don't wrap around at all.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives, sessile bellwort has the most understated appearance - largeflower bellwort has much bigger, showier blooms, while perfoliate bellwort has distinctive leaves that completely surround the stem like the stem is poking through them.
Unlike sessile bellwort, which has leaves that clasp the stem but aren't pierced by it, perfoliate bellwort's stem actually passes through the leaf base.
